newsitem.title: USA: Alyeska spill blamed on water-treatment plant.
newsitem.headline: Alyeska spill blamed on water-treatment plant.

text.p: A malfunction in the trans-Alaska pipeline's ballast-water-treatment plant probably caused a patchy oil sheen that emerged Friday at the system's Valdez port, a state official said Tuesday.

The treatment plant was switched over the weekend to a "recycle" mode -- with no ballast water being discharged or effluent released into the port -- to allow officials to investigate the cause of the problem, said Leslie Pearson, on-scene cleanup coordinator for the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation.

Although oil shipments resumed Saturday, tankers arriving at the Valdez terminal must retain their loads of oily ballast water that are carried to balance the ships during the transist north, Pearson said.
"The vessels that are coming in and loading are presently not deballasting. So they have to go back south with a short load," she said.
Oil tankers have been departing Valdez with crude loads about 20 percent to 30 percent smaller than normal, Pearson said.
The ballast-water-treatment plant was fingered after inspectors cleared the three oil tankers docked at the port from blame for the sheen of weathered oil discovered on the water surface.
New sheens continually appeared until after the effluent discharge was stopped Sunday afternoon, Pearson said.
"That, to me, reflects that the source of this spill was from the ballast-water-treatment plant," she said.

No shoreline or animals were affected by the oil leak, said Alyeska Pipeline Service Co., operator of the trans-Alaska pipeline system. In all, about 26 gallons of oil were collected during the cleanup, Alyeska said.

One of the terminal's four oil-loading berths was closed Monday, Pearson said. Berth 3, in the path of the effluent outfall, was blocked off to allow officials to investigate the ballast-water-treatment problem, she said.
The cause of the system malfunction was unknown Tuesday, Pearson said.
